messages.subject_clean: Larger uncertainty in multiseason model vs single season + mirrored detection probabilities
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jamie,

Happy New Year! As you mention, this is a complicated question without any one specific answer, and the utility of multi-season approaches versus independent single season models depends on objectives, data, etc. Here are some thoughts on your current example to try to help you reason through the patterns you're seeing:
When using tPGOcc, are you including ar1 = TRUE? Or alternatively, are you including a random unstructured season effect on occupancy probability? If you are, then the results don't surprise me too much, particularly since you have only four levels (seasons) of the random effect. Because of this, there will be large uncertainty in the estimates of that random effect, which will then subsequently lead to uncertainty in the estimated occupancy probabilities. Even if there are more seasons, it would certainly not be impossible for uncertainty of seasonal occupancy estimates in a multi-season model to be larger. Part of what a multi-season model is doing is accounting for non-independence in occupancy probability over time. When ignoring any type of non-independence (e.g., temporal autocorrelation, spatial autocorrelation, or classical "pseudoreplication"), uncertainty is underestimated. Thus, when accounting for that non-independence, the uncertainty in estimates can increase. Of course, depending on what you are doing, this may not result in estimates from one model compared to another being more or less precise, but needless to say, it is certainly possible to have larger uncertainty in a multi-season model (particularly when including a season random effect with only a few levels). If you remove the ar1 random effect (or the unstructured effect), you will likely see patterns that more so arise with what you predicted.
Note that spOccupancy by default in multi-season models in the "out$psi.samples" component will provide predictions for non-sampled site/season combinations (e.g., estimates of psi at site 1 in season 2 will be predicted even if that site was not sampled in that season). Because of this, when comparing average occupancy estimates from multi-season to single-season estimates, you should make sure that each annual occupancy estimate from the multi-season model is only using data from those sites that are sampled in that season, and not the predictions (which will have larger uncertainty).
The differences in the patterns of detection probabilities could arise for multiple reasons. In the multi-season model, if you have covariates on detection probability, the effect of those covariates is likely assumed to be constant across the four seasons (unless you explicitly included an interaction with season and the covariate in the formula). When fitting single season models, this relationship is estimated separately for each season, which could result in differences in that relationship by seasons (the same goes for occupancy values). This could lead to the differences in the patterns you observe (and could also explain differences in the occupancy patterns). The actual interpretation of any variation in these relationships over the seasons (e.g., if it's actually an ecological/observational pattern or if any variation is just a result of randomness) is something you would need to assess based on your expertise of the system.
Sorry for the long and not super clear message, but hopefully it helps give you some things to think about. Perhaps others will have some thoughts as well.

Cheers,

Jeff

messages.subject: spMsPGOcc - difficulty with convergence
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm having some trouble getting the spatial covariates of a spMsPGOcc model to converge, and was hoping for some guidance.

I'm fitting the model below with data from 53 sites and 28 species. Currently the community-level means and variances all appear to converge, and at the species-level all occurrence, detection, and phi spatial covariance variables appear to converge, but there are always 3-4 species for which sigma.sq does not converge (rhat >1.1).

Do I just need to increase the number of samples? I know the vignette says these are some of the most computationally intensive models and may take hours or days to run (this model took ~8 hours). I also thought about changing the initial sigma.sq values - would this help? Is there something else I haven't considered?

 Any guidance would be appreciated!

msom.occ.null1.spatial6 <- spMsPGOcc(occ.formula = ~ scale(dist_to_edge) + scale(dist_to_roads) + scale(X500_FC_PER),
                                     det.formula = ~1,
                                     data = data.msom,
                                     n.batch = 60000, # *25 = 1,500,000 samples
                                     batch.length = 25,
                                     accept.rate = 0.43,
                                     cov.model = "exponential",
                                     n.omp.threads = 1,
                                     verbose = TRUE,
                                     NNGP = TRUE,
                                     n.neighbors = 5,
                                     n.report = 10000,
                                     n.burn = 500000,
                                     n.thin = 50,
                                     n.chains = 3,
)

Best wishes,
Tasha

(P.S. Thanks to Jeff for developing this package :) )

messages.subject: Re: spMsPGOcc - difficulty with convergence
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tasha,

spMsPGOcc models can be quite difficult to work with, particularly for communities larger than 5-10 species or so, and when some of your species are quite rare. In general, I now recommend using the "spatial factor multispecies occupancy" (sfMsPGOcc) model approach as opposed to spMsPGOcc given that it: (1) is substantially faster; (2) performs equally as well or better than spMsPGOcc in a variety of situations as shown in the paper I link to in the next sentence; (3) and often will be easier to get to converge than spMsPGOcc unless you have ideal circumstances (e.g., only a few species and not super rare). So, I might suggest trying sfMsPGocc instead, which is described in depth in this vignette <https://doserlab.com/files/spoccupancy-web/articles/factormodels> and this paper. <https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ecy.4137> Here are a couple other things to think about as well.
53 sites is a relatively small number of sites to use for a complex spatial occupancy model, so fitting any sort of spatial model will likely be difficult. Because there are not all that many spatial locations, there is limited information that is available to the model to try and estimate the spatial parameters, which is likely why convergence is leading to difficulties. The spMsPGocc function estimates a separate spatial random effect for each species, which is very difficult to do, even when there are a substantially larger number of spatial locations (e.g., hundreds). This is further reason to try out the sfMsPGOcc function, as it will likely be easier to estimate than spMsPGOcc.
I see are not including any covariates on detection probability. If there is unmodeled heterogeneity in detection probability, this could also contribute to spatial models being difficult to converge, so that could be something else to think about if you continue to not get the models to work.
It may also be helpful to ensure that non-spatial models (e.g., msPGOcc) can converge successfully before going to far down a rabbit hole with convergence issues in the spatial model. Sometimes you may just have too many rare species that you are trying to model.
Setting initial values is always useful, particularly for the spatial parameters. Whether you continue with spMsPGOcc or go to sfMsPGOcc, setting initial values based on the values of a preliminary run can often help with convergence difficulties. This vignette <https://doserlab.com/files/spoccupancy-web/articles/modelconsiderations> talks about some convergence problems with different types of spatial occupancy models.
 Hope that helps!

Jeff

messages.subject: Re: spMsPGOcc - difficulty with convergence
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tasha,

Glad to hear you were able to get the model to converge. The large uncertainty is likely related to the fairly small number of spatial locations used to fit the spatial model. Spatial occupancy models can be data hungry, particularly when it comes to having a large number of sites, so fitting a model with 53 sites may show substantial uncertainty in the model parameters as a result and will often perform worse with cross-validation (since that requires fitting models with an even smaller number of spatial locations). I think it is reasonable to conclude that you can continue with msPGOcc given the small number of sites and hence difficulty to estimate a spatial process, the cross-validation results, and large uncertainty in the factor loadings.

Kind regards,

Jeff

Hi All,

I'm using the spOccupancy package to fit a single-species occupancy model (PGOcc function) to assess sun bear occupancy across Borneo. In line with our expectations, the model outputs indicate that forest cover and human population pressure are influential determinants of sun bear occurrence - sun bears are more likely to occur in forested areas free from human influence.

However, issues arise when attempting to map spatial predictions of sun bear occurrence values across a wider geographic area. Despite identifying a positive relationship with forest cover, deforested areas (cells with a proportion of 0 to 0.3 forest cover) are predicted to have the highest occupancy for sun bears (psi=0.999).

Based on my initial attempts to diagnose the problem, this issue seems to relate to how the raster's used in the spatial predictions are scaled. When I follow the online tutorial [https://doserlab.com/files/spoccupancy-web/articles/modelfitting], by scaling rasters using the mean and standard deviation derived from the observed covariate values across sampling locations ((forest21_df$val - mean(data.ssom$occ.covs$mean_forest)) /  sd(data.ssom$occ.covs$mean_forest)) , spatial predictions derived from the predict function become unreliable in deforested areas and seem to follow the opposite trend depicted on the caterpillar plots of covariate associations (MCMCplot(out$beta.samples, ref_ovl = TRUE, ci = c(75, 95)))).

However, if I scale the same rasters using R's scale function (forest21.0 <- scale(forest21_df$val) (as I did for the covariates in the initial model), the predict function produces a map that more accurately reflects the observed relationship between occurrence and forest cover - though I'm not entirely sure this is the correct approach.

I have a feeling this could be due to my forest values in my data being skewed towards 1 (as camera-traps are typically placed in forested areas).
Any advice you could offer to diagnose this issue would be much appreciated. I'm not sure if I'm overlooking something in my code or if this reflects a broader underlying issue. Please let me know if a more reproducible example is needed.

# Then get the quantiles of psi.0.mean.samples
psi.0.quants <- apply(psi.0.mean.samples, 2, quantile, prob = c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))

messages.body_plain:
Hi Katie,

Thanks for sending the data offline! After looking at the code and output, it looks to me like the approach where you use mean() and sd() to standardize the covariates for prediction is actually giving you the correct results, and there isn't any problem with conversions from rasters to data frames. Looking at your model output, you do have a significant positive linear effect of forest cover, but notice also that you have a significant positive quadratic effect. This corresponds to the model estimating a "U" shaped relationship with forest cover, where occupancy probability peaks at low values and then at high values, so there is not just an estimated positive linear relationship with forest cover. So, given those results, the results of the first graph (that uses the standardization approach I outline in the vignette) actually gives results that line up with what the output of the model suggests.

When you use scale() in "occ.formula" when fitting the model, the covariates are scaled by the mean and standard deviation of the covariate values at the observed locations. When doing this, any predictions you subsequently do must scale the covariates by the same values, otherwise the covariates will be on different scales. In your case, the mean of the covariates of forest cover at observed locations is about 0.96 with an sd of 0.11, while the mean of forest cover at prediction locations is about 0.73 with an sd of 0.36. Notice that these are different from the observed values. When you just use scale() on the prediction locations, this standardizes the values with the prediction means and sd, which are different from the observed values, and thus the observed covariates and prediction covariates aren't on the same scales and the results from such a prediction aren't valid.

Let me know if I can clarify any of this.

Cheers,

Jeff

Hi Julien,

Glad you were able to figure this out. Yes, the length of the offset should be equal to the number of sites.

As an aside, 3 species is not really enough to fit a regular multi-species model as the default is implemented, since species-level effects are treated as random effects. Thus, with only three species, you only have three levels to estimate a variance parameter, which is not much information. Instead, you could fit a separate model for each species, or if you wanted to fit all together I would suggest setting the tags "independent.betas" and "independent.alphas" = TRUE in the prior list, which will separately estimate species-specific effects. See this thread <https://groups.google.com/g/hmecology/c/0HWn7OemeRo/m/R6mIqz10AQAJ> from the HMecology google group a while back on how to go about doing that and let me know if you have any questions.

Hi Mic and Naomi,

Thanks for the questions. The answers to your two questions are slightly different, so I'll respond one at a time:

Mic

This is interesting and I'm not exactly sure what is going on here just by looking at the code. First, as always, make sure you have the latest version installed from CRAN (0.8.0) because there's a chance this is related to a small memory problem I fixed a while back (although that is wishful thinking). The fact that you tested with only one year and one site and still got the error indicates to me there could be a bug in the underlying function. I don't think many folks have used this function before, so this could be something I haven't come upon yet. Would you be able to send me a reproducible example? I don't need the actual output from the spOccupancy run (e.g., the out.svc list), but if you can send the data in data.list and the data you were using for predictions so I can generate the error that would be super helpful for predicting.

Also, as an aside, setting "n.omp.threads = 40" will actually likely slow the model down. The way the parallelization works, there is usually an optimum number of threads to set the values to that's usually around 10 or so, although it can vary depending on machine and data set. Regardless, I'd recommend bringing that down a bit to around 10 or so.

Naomi

When doing prediction over a large number of sites, the objects that the model needs to create are quite large (i.e., for spPGOcc a matrix with rows equal to the number of MCMC locations and columns equal to the number of sites). The way it's coded in spOccupancy requires these objects to be stored in continuous memory, which means that even if the object is not bigger than the amount of RAM on the computer, it may still run out of storage if it can't find enough continuous memory to store things. Long story short, the simplest way to get around this is to predict for a small amount of locations at a time, generate some summary output from those predictions, store those summaries in an array, and do this a bunch of times until you succeed for the whole prediction set. I talked a bit about this in a previous thread here <https://groups.google.com/g/spocc-spabund-users/c/uoRUji5vkUQ>. Try out that approach to see if that works, and if it doesn't then let me know. d

Jeff
